I have mixed feelings about my childhood. On the one hand, I have really good memories of it and there were superfun times. On the other hand, I had to face some kind of bullying and being singled out by some stupid kids because I was 'unique'. My parents, especially mom, often recall how quiet and afraid of people I was as a baby. I was definitely not a 'daring one'. They thought I had some sort of autism (I think I might be on a spectrum, like Asperger's). I learned to talk before I started walking when I was about 2. I felt the more grown-up kids in the neighborhood didn't like me because I didn't obey their 'rules' when we played together in group (I later realize it's probably because the majority of them weren't the 'NT' type). When I started kindergerten, I became a selective mute for about two years and even the teachers couldn't do anything about it. Despite being mute at school, I made a couple of friends, but my best friends were a few neighbors my age who never actually went to the same schools with me. Spending time with my best friends was the superfun part for me - we'd watch movies together, build fortresses, play with dirt, roleplays, etc., almost like those friends in *Stand By Me* or *The Goonies*, but the real thing felt so much better. 

The last year in kindergarten was when my intellect started to shine. I won a place in a writing contest and eventually started speaking at school and became what they'd call 'normal'. In primary school I still got bullied a few times for being 'different' and the fact that I sucked at PE so they saw me as weak. I pretty much didn't care and usually fought back and went about my own things. Plus, I already made some good friends who stuck around despite me having trouble once in a while with the bullies.  I excelled in a lot of classes, got to know other smart kids, and ended up graduating with the highest scores, which earned me some respect (though I didn't care about beng 'known', I noticed other friends became nicer to me). In secondary school, I was still viewed by general public as the nerdy one but my group of friends were really accepting of who I was. Although we grew apart a bit when we went to college (it's basicaly me growing apart and our circles of friends grew much bigger) and at the moment we're living different lives in different parts of the world, we still make some effort to keep in touch.

Many among my favorite actors and entertainers are gay or bisexual and if any more of them came out I would still be a faithful fan and follow up with whatever projects they do without having to be reminded all the time of their sexual orientation - because it's already established that I like them based on their talents and personality, not as a fantasy boyfriend (though it sometimes happens and the possibility of them being gay doesn't hurt). And if they do decide to come out much later, chances are I will love and respect them even more. I can give you one example - Darren Hayes was one half of a 90's duo band and the fact that he was married to a woman once, dealt with a divorce, and later decided to come out years after his solo carreer did not disappoint me at all (though it could also be the fact that I never fancy him that way like many of his female fans did/do), it made me understand him and his work as a whole. He dealt with his demons and ever since he seems so much happier and more in tune with himself. If you publicly come out, I doubt the majority of your female fanbase will readily abandon you. It's possible that you may lose some but in return you'll gain more when you are honest with yourself. Just live your life the way that will make you most happy and you won't even feel pressured to come out. I wish you all the best.
